segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? Should we continue in sin so that grace may increase?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Certainly not! We who died to sin, how can we still live in it?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if we have become united with the likeness of his death, we will certainly also be united with that of his resurrection.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We know this: our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, and we might no longer be slaves to sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one who has died has been justified from sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: since we know that Christ, raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer has mastery over him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way, you too must count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey the body's desires,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and do not go on presenting the parts of your body to sin as weapons of unrighteousness. Instead, present yourselves to God as people alive from the dead, and the parts of your body to God as weapons of righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For sin will not have mastery over you, since you are not under law but under grace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then? Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? Certainly not!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not know that if you present yourselves to someone as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But thanks be to God that you, who were slaves of sin, obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that, set free from sin, you were enslaved to righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, leading to more lawlessness, so now present the parts of your body as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with regard to righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So what fruit did you have then from the things you are now ashamed of? For the end of those things is death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now, set free from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit, leading to holiness, and the end is eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

notes.phrase: united with the likeness of his death
notes.traditional: united with him in the likeness of his death
notes.note: The Greek adjective means 'grown together, joined'. Many translations supply 'with him' and take 'the likeness of his death' as the manner of the union. The Greek has no 'with him', and the rendering here takes 'the likeness' as the thing believers are joined to; both readings are grammatically possible. The second half of the verse is compressed in Greek ('but also of the resurrection') and 'united with that of' is supplied from the first half.

The verb means to make something ineffective or put it out of operation, and can extend to abolishing it altogether. Older versions have 'destroyed'; the rendering here keeps the commoner sense, that the body as sin's possession loses its hold, without implying the physical body is annihilated.

Most English versions render 'freed' or 'set free' here, but the verb is Paul's ordinary word for 'justify' (declare in the right, acquit), from the same word-family as 'righteousness' later in the chapter. A different verb for 'set free' appears in verses 18 and 22. The sense is probably that death settles sin's legal claim on a person; many scholars think Paul is adapting a general maxim that death clears all debts. That it amounts to release from sin's power is a fair inference, which is why the traditional rendering exists.

The traditional 'instruments' is possible, since the word can mean a tool, but its usual sense is 'weapon', and it clearly means that elsewhere in Paul's letters (Romans 13:12; 2 Corinthians 6:7; 10:4). The military picture fits the context, with sin 'reigning' in verse 12 and paying a soldier's 'wages' in verse 23. Many commentators prefer 'weapons', though most English versions keep 'instruments'.

notes.phrase: to which you were handed over
notes.note: Some older versions reverse the construction so that the teaching is delivered to the believers. The Greek says the believers were handed over to the teaching, which fits the chapter's picture of slaves transferred from one master to another. The verb is also the usual one for passing on tradition, and Paul may intend that echo.

notes.phrase: from the things you are now ashamed of
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and the sentence can be divided differently: 'So what fruit did you have then? Things of which you are now ashamed.' On that reading Paul answers his own question; on the reading adopted here the implied answer is 'none'. Editors and translators are divided.

The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering and is kept; a minority of translators render 'life of the age to come'.

The word was used especially for a soldier's pay or ration-money, continuing the military picture of verse 13. Sin pays out what has been earned. The contrasting word, 'gift', is related to 'grace' and denotes something given freely, not earned.

candidates.reason: Frequent in Paul and rendered variously as destroy, abolish, nullify, bring to nothing or set aside, which hides that one verb is in play across Romans, 1–2 Corinthians and Galatians.
The choice between 'slave' and 'servant' (with δουλεύω and δουλόω) affects every book and should be settled once.
Translations vary between 'sanctification', 'holiness' and 'consecration', and the choice should match the rendering of the ἅγιος word-family elsewhere.
Central in Romans 4 and elsewhere, rendered reckon, count, credit, consider or impute; readers need to see it is one verb.
No register entry was supplied for this chapter; the choice between 'flesh', 'human nature', 'sinful nature' and 'body' is heavily contested and needs one policy.
